messages.subject: Progress bar for parallelized HMC
messages.subject_clean: Progress bar for parallelized HMC
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am running three HMC chains in parallel using parLapply() with the nimbleHMC functions in a workflow similar to this one: https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/parallelizing_NIMBLE.html

However, with a reasonable number of iterations, computation time is still tremendous due to the complexity of my model. I would thus like to have a progress bar displayed while the HMC chains run in parallel. Alternatively, an a priori calculation of the approximate total computation time would be a good start.

I have tried several things, such as replacing parLapply() with pblapply() from the pbapply package or future_lapply() from the future.apply package, which would display a progress bar, but that one is useless, as it just jumps from 0% to 100% at once, when the operation has finished.

Did anyone come up with a good way of getting a progress bar while running MCMC (or HMC) chains in parallel?

Cheers,

Leander

Dear all,
I have gone through the problem of having no more space on my disk under Windows after having used Nimble repeatedly in a simulation context. The problem seems to be due to the creation of Rtmp... files containing a folder named "nimble_GeneratedCode". This subfloder contains 5 dll files in my case, that are between 1 & 2 Mo size each. In total I had 280 Go used by these folders.

Is there a way to remove automatically - or through a Nimble command - these folders after use?

Sincerely,

Frédéric

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am facing a problem, I think the problem is with initialization, can you please help me with that?
The model is working when my forklength data range between say, 200 to 300. But, when my length is 500 - 800, it is not working. I am little bit confused.

Here is the code:
library(nimble)
library(MCMCvis)
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)

#' Read in the data.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------#
cap_data <- read.csv("simulated_capture.csv")
dd_fl <- read.csv("simulated_forklength.csv")

y <- cap_data %>%
  select(Fall_2014:Fall_2020) %>%
  #select(year_2014:year_2020) %>%
  as.matrix()
#head(y)

dd_fl <- dd_fl %>%
  select(Fall_2014: Fall_2020) %>%
  as.matrix()
dd_fl[dd_fl == 0] <- NA
#head(dd_fl)

#Scaling the forklength
#-----------------------------------------------------------------------#

# Define a function to scale each row separately
logscale_row <- function(row) {
  # Filter out NA values
  row_without_nas <- row[!is.na <http://is.na>(row)]
  # Scale the row
  logscaled_row <- log(row_without_nas)
  # Replace NA positions with NA in scaled row
  logscaled_row_with_nas <- rep(NA, length(row))
  logscaled_row_with_nas[!is.na <http://is.na>(row)] <- logscaled_row
  return(logscaled_row_with_nas)
}

# Apply the scaling function to each row of the forklength
d_fl <- t(apply(dd_fl, 1, logscale_row))

#d_fl <- dd_fl

#head(d_fl)

#' Get occasion of first capture.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------#
get.first <- function(x) min(which(x != 0))
first <- apply(y, 1, get.first)
#first

# Nimble Code
#------------------------------------------------------------------------#

code_m <- nimbleCode({
  # Priors

  alpha[1] ~ dnorm(0,0.1)
  alpha[2] ~ dnorm(0,0.1)

  beta[1] ~ dnorm(0,0.1)
  beta[2] ~ dnorm(0,0.1)

  p.male ~ dbeta(1,1)

  a_sigma <- 0.001
  b_sigma <- 1000

  sigma ~ dinvgamma(a_sigma, b_sigma)

  Linf_mu <- 5.5
  VBk_mu <- 0
  Ind_mu <- 0

  tau_Linf <- 0.1
  tau_k <- 0.1
  tau_Ind <- 0.1

  ## priors for VB growth parameters

  # asymptotic size - male or female
  a ~  T(dnorm(6.8, 0.1), 0, 7) # Anadromous DV's length as always lies between 300 (ln(300) = 5.7) to 900 (ln(900) = 6.8).

  # growth coefficient - male or female

  k ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)

  # individual heterogeneity in growth parameter - lambda - male or female
  lambda ~ T(dnorm(0, 0.1),0,)

  for (i in 1:N) {

    # first capture
    P[i,first[i]] <- lambda*H_m[i,first[i]] # this multiplies individual heterogeneity (lambda) by expected fl
    H_m[i,first[i]] ~ dunif(5.5,6.75)   # expected size of animal at unknown age at first capture

    for (t in (first[i]+1):nyears) {

      fl[i,t] ~ T(dnorm(fl[i,t-1]+increment[i,t],sigma), fl[i,t-1],a)
      increment[i,t] ~ dgamma(P[i,t]+0.01,lambda) # offset to prevent model from getting stuck
      P[i,t] <- lambda*abs(H_m[i,t]-H_m[i,t-1])
      H_m[i,t] <- H_m[i,t-1] + (a - H_m[i,t-1])*(1-exp(-k))  # VB Model
    }

    # Multistate-Modelling

    # Initial state
    z[i,first[i]] <- y[i,first[i]] - 1

    for (t in (first[i]+1):nyears) {
      # State transition
      z[i, t] ~ dcat(px[z[i, t - 1], 1:2, i, t])

      # Observation process
      y[i, t] ~ dcat(po[z[i, t], 1:2, i, t])
    }
  }

  # probabilities of state z(t+1) given z(t)
  for (i in 1:N) {

    for (t in first[i]:nyears) {

      logit(phi[i, t]) <- alpha[1] + (alpha[2]*fl[i, t])
      logit(p[i, t]) <- beta[1] + (beta[2]*fl[i,t])

      # Latent state process probabilities
      px[1, 1, i, t] <- phi[i,t]
      px[1, 2, i, t] <- 1 - phi[i,t]

      px[2, 1, i, t] <- 0
      px[2, 2, i, t] <- 1

      # Observation process probabilities
      po[1, 1, i, t] <- 1 - p[i,t]
      po[1, 2, i, t] <- p[i,t]

      po[2, 1, i, t] <- 1
      po[2, 2, i, t] <- 0

    }
  }
})

#Input Data
#-----------------------------------------------------------------------#
my.data = list(y=y + 1, fl = d_fl)

#Constants in a list.
#-----------------------------------------------------------------------#
N = nrow(y)
nyears = ncol(y)

my.constants <- list(N = N, nyears = nyears, first = first)

# Generate inits for the latent states
#-----------------------------------------------------------------------#

# Initializing fl

fl_inits_temp <- dd_fl

replace_nas_increasing_order <- function(row) {
  na_indices <- which(is.na <http://is.na>(row))

  for (i in na_indices) {
    if (i == 1) {
      row[i] <- row[i + 1] + 1
    } else if (i == length(row)) {
      row[i] <- row[i - 1] + 1
    } else {
      # Adjust the range to handle consecutive NAs
      start_range <- ifelse(!is.finite(row[i - 1]), 0, row[i - 1] + 1)
      end_range <- ifelse(!is.finite(row[i + 1]), start_range + 1, row[i + 1] - 1)

      if (!is.finite(start_range) || !is.finite(end_range)) {
        row[i] <- row[i - 1] + 1
      } else {
        row[i] <- sample(seq(start_range, end_range), 1)
      }
    }
  }

  return(row)
}

fl_inits_1 <- apply(fl_inits_temp, 1, replace_nas_increasing_order)

fl_inits_2 <- t(fl_inits_1)

#head(fl_inits_1)
#head(fl_inits_2)

# Function to replace values in Matrix B with NAs based on NAs in Matrix A
replace_values_with_nas <- function(matrix_a, matrix_b) {
  # Get the indices where Matrix A has NAs
  na_indices <- which(!is.na <http://is.na>(matrix_a), arr.ind = TRUE)

  # Replace values in Matrix B with NAs at the corresponding positions
  matrix_b[na_indices] <- NA

  return(matrix_b)
}

d_fl_inits <- replace_values_with_nas(fl_inits_temp, fl_inits_2)

d_fl_inits <- as.matrix(d_fl_inits)

head(d_fl_inits)

for (i in 1:N){
  if (first[i] == 1) next
  if (first[i] > 1) d_fl_inits[i,1:(first[i]-1)] <- NA
}

#head(d_fl_inits)

# Apply the scaling function to each row of the initial forklength
fl_inits <- t(apply(d_fl_inits, 1, logscale_row))
#fl_inits <- d_fl_inits
#head(fl_inits)
#tail(fl_inits)
#------------------------------------------------------------------------#
# Initializing alive state

x.init <- matrix(1, N, nyears)  # Set to 1 or another appropriate value for initial state
for (i in 1:N) {
  if (first[i] > 1) x.init[i, 1:(first[i]-1)] <- NA
}

z_inits <- x.init
#head(z_inits)
#------------------------------------------------------------------------#

increment_inits <- matrix(runif(N * nyears), nrow = N, ncol = nyears)

#head(mu_inits)

#------------------------------------------------------------------------#

H_m_inits <- matrix(runif(N * nyears, 5.5, 6.75), nrow = N, ncol = nyears)

#------------------------------------------------------------------------#

#------------------------ Final initialization --------------------------#

initial.values <- list(alpha = runif(2, 0, 1), beta = runif(2,0,1),
                       a = runif(1,3,9), k = runif(1, 0, 1), lambda = runif(1,0,1),
                      increment = increment_inits, H_m = H_m_inits,
                       sigma = runif(1, 0, 10), a_sigma = 0.001, b_sigma = 1000,
                      p.male=0.3, fl = fl_inits, z = z_inits)

#' Parameters to monitor.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------#
parameters.to.save <- c("alpha", "beta", "a","k","lambda","sigma")

#' MCMC settings.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------#
n.iter <- 400
n.burnin <- 50
n.chains <- 2

mcmc.nim_model <- nimbleModel(code = code_m,
                              constants = my.constants,
                              data = my.data,
                              inits = initial.values)
mcmc.nim_model$calculate()

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian, I haven't fully absorbed what you're doing here and haven't looked in detail at your code, but one reaction is as follows.

If the projection part of the model doesn't involve any data (i.e., it is pure posterior simulation given the parameters fitted in the IPM part of the model), then a good strategy would be to fit the IPM part of the model to get samples from the posterior of the IPM parameters and then run the projection for each posterior sample. This could be done in parallel in R without using nimble, or you could use nimbleFunctions to do the projection (this could also be done in parallel, so long as you build the model and compile it any nimbleFunctions separately in each parallel worker). So the second stage would not actually be running an MCMC because you wouldn't be conditioning directly on any data.

It sounds like you may already have satisfactory mixing in not-too-long for the IPM part of the model, so you may be in a good position to not have to worry further about MCMC mixing, but simply deal with the projection part by "brute force".

Daniel's suggestion for the `prior_samples` sampler would be useful if you did actually have data that were directly part of the projection model.

-chris

On Tue, Dec 31, 2024 at 5:35 AM Daniel Turek <danie...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Brian, a quick note about your (1) Can I add posterior draws from the IPM to the PVA so parameters are already converged and just simulate from those for the PVA part? This would be easiest to implement and fastest. Is this possible?
>
> The "prior_samples" sampler was added to the MCMC a few releases ago, which should accomplish what you want - using posterior draws (stored in a numeric vector or array) as the prior for a model parameter.  I'll copy the documentation for it below, but let me know if you have questions or problems with it.
>
> Your other suggestions are all viable as well, in particular the vectorization, and using nimbleFunctions to move around how/where computation takes place.
>
> Cheers,
> Daniel
>
> #' @section prior_samples sampler:
> #'
> #' The prior_samples sampler uses a provided set of numeric values (\code{samples}) to define the prior distribution of one or more model nodes.  One every MCMC iteration, the prior_samples sampler takes value(s) from the numeric values provided, and stores these value(s) into the target model node(s).  This allows one to define the prior distribution of model parameters empirically, using a set of numeric \code{samples}, presumably obtained previously using MCMC.  The \code{target} node may be either a single scalar node (scalar case), or a collection of model nodes.
> #'
> #' The prior_samples sampler provides two options for selection of the value to use on each MCMC iteration.  The default behaviour is to take sequential values from the \code{samples} vector (scalar case), or in the case of multiple dimensions, sequential rows of the \code{samples} matrix are used.  The alternative behaviour, by setting the control argument \code{randomDraws = TRUE}, will instead use random draws from the \code{samples} vector (scalar case), or randomly selected rows of the \code{samples} matrix in the multidimensional case.
> #'
> #' If the default of sequential selection of values is used, and the number of MCMC iterations exceeds the length of the \code{samples} vector (scalar case) or the number of rows of the \code{samples} matrix, then \code{samples} will be recycled as necessary for the number of MCMC iterations.  A message to this effect is also printed at the beginning of the MCMC chain.
> #'

messages.body_plain:
Hi Leander,

Without investigating how to pass output from the parallel workers back to the main R session, I think the easiest path will be an a priori calculation of total computation time.

Once the HMC warmup period is over, the computation time should scale roughly linearly with the number of iterations unless the chain gets "stuck" for periods of time in certain problematic parts of the space in which the NUTS sampler tree depths are large.  So if you have an idea of a sufficient warmup length, you could do something like the following to get an estimate:

Suppose the warmup length is 500.

1) Run a chain for 500 total iterations (including warmup) with a warmup of 500 to be able to time just the warmup.
2) Run a separate chain for 1500 total iterations with a warmup of 500.
3) Subtract the times and divide by 1000 to estimate the time per iteration after warmup.

-chris

Perhaps things are different on Windows, but in my experience on Linux/MacOS when an R session ends, its Rtmp directory should be removed and no longer take up space. Perhaps Windows R behaves differently or something is going wrong with the cleanup when you close the R session.

If necessary, you can manually remove the files in the `nimble_generatedCode` directory from within R like this:

```
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "nimble_generatedCode")
for(file in list.files(path)) {
 file.remove(file.path(path, file))
}
```

(There might be a way to remove entire directory with some flag related to recursiveness, but I didn't see it when I looked quickly at R's file-handling functions.)

-chris

I want to follow up on this issue from the fall. In our work on a new nimble version in December, I realized I had mis-diagnosed the problem you were encountering here. The slice sampler was working fine. The problem was a minor but verbose issue with nimbleHMC. We have also in December released an updated version of nimbleHMC that fixes this. If you are still working on this model, please try updating both nimble and nimbleHMC and see if the problem is resolved. The previous fix shouldn't have been necessary. Thanks for reporting the issue.
Perry

Hi David,

Thanks for the report. What a curious situation. C++ warnings and errors can be compiler- or OS-dependent, and that seems to be the case here. The error is coming from nimble-generated C++ while building your vignette, which explains why we don't see it when we submit new versions of nimble. From the path label "CRAN_special_gcc-san" in the CRAN output, it looks like it is running a sanitizer version of a C++ compiler, which would be instrumented to catch errors where a regular version might not, with the possibility of false positives. I somewhat doubt the error is a real problem because otherwise something would likely not be working, or could even be crashing. In any case, here are two possible work-arounds for you.

The error is coming from this line of your resizeVector method:

xPrev     = nimNumeric(length=lengthOri, value=x[1:lengthOri])

In this case, you should be able instead to do simply:

xPrev = x[1:lengthOri]

Assignment to the full object xPrev should allocate it as well as assign the values.

If that doesn't satisfy CRAN-checking, another option is this trick <https://ropensci.org/blog/2019/12/08/precompute-vignettes/> for getting vignette code run on your machine before submitting to CRAN, so all that happens on CRAN is building the vignette without running code.

Meanwhile I'll file an issue for us to look at what is happening and see if we can "fix" it (in quotes because it might not be broken but is nevertheless a potential pain for others).

Perry

messages.subject_clean: Crazy Coefficiants in My Occupancy Model
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm having a model fitting issue and I'm hoping someone has some ideas. It involves a hierarchical binary regression model.

Data
I'm working with occupancy data (i.e. modeling species P(occupancy) and P(detection|occupancy). Here's a good primer if you're unfamiliar.
https://kevintshoemaker.github.io/NRES-746/Occupancy.html

Goal
I want to implement some new techniques from my dissertation work. This requires writing my own occupancy model  from scratch instead of using an existing occupancy packages. This should be pretty straightforward.

Issue
My basic occupancy model has regression coefficients blasting off to negative or positive infinity in situations where frequentest from the unmarked package and the nimble-based spOccupancy models do fine. This issue only arises in the occupancy part of the model, which makes sense to me because it is "further" from the data than the detection part. I've tried implementing a Pólya-gamma sampler as well, but issues remain. Here are the conclusions:
    1) Generally, unmarked and spOcc do pretty good
    2) My method with flat priors goes crazy when modeling occupancy, with the intercept and the other coeffs going far in different directions.
    3) PG sampling controls the intercept in a bit, but destroys power of test in other predictors (all close to 0)

Code is attached.

Thank you,
Jacob

Hey Jacob,

I see several issues.

First, you need to give initial values to all stochastic nodes in Nimble. Just looking at your most basic model (pg.sam = F), you're missing initial values for z.rand. You can check this with:  n_model$initializeInfo()

The other issue that immediately jumps out is that you are using a flat prior for terms that end up going through logit transformations. I think John just mentioned this as well. Here's a great paper on that: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13407

A good way to think about priors, beyond just choosing ones that are scale-invariant (aka look good when transformed), is to use a prior predictive check. Try running your model without provided y, but providing initial values for y (so essentially without data). You'll see what the posterior for p looks like and be able to make more informed prior decisions from there.

As a general rule, dnorm(0, .3) is a good place to start (a normal with mean 0 and an sd of sqrt(1/.3)), but you will need to adapt.

Hope these help.

-Heather Gaya

Okay, on second glance your issue is actually that you've set up occupancy incorrectly.

I see you have z (true occupancy state) set up as:

z.rand[i] ~ dbern(p[i])#presence
 z[i] <- conf.pres[i] + (1-conf.pres[i])*z.rand[i]

This is not what you want. p is the probability that the site is occupied. You want the model to decide on this for itself.

I would put the dbern directly on z:
z[i] ~ dbern(p[i]).
and later:
y[i] ~ dbern(z[i]*p.det[i])

If z = 0, you cannot get a y of 1, so for all sites where something was detected, the model will know z = 1. For all other sites, it'll model if the site is truly occupied or not.

I've attached a code with a working version of your model and an example of using a prior predictive check to see what kind of prior will be reasonable after undergoing the logit.

Hi Miki,

Thanks for posting the question.

I can't run your code because I don't have your `data` or your `d_log_inf`.

Can you clarify what you're trying to do here? With nimble's RJ tools, managed at a high level from configureRJ and implemented in several nimbleFunctions, you wouldn't need to write your own. Of course you can, but I am not sure if they are trying to provide different functionality.

Can you say what version of nimble you're using? I'd suggest either providing a fully reproducible example (you can share data off-list if you prefer) or clarifying your goals.

Post-processing results from RJ can sometimes be confusing at first because you'll have a chain that sometimes sits at zero and sometimes samples a non-zero posterior region.

For reference on this thread, the published version of the paper you linked seems to be here <https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.2020.1826955>.

Perry

My understanding is that the algorithm alternates between the two variables: proposing to add a parameter if it is zero, or proposing to remove it if it is nonzero. From my reading (https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.01340), this approach resembles "nonreversible jump" MCMC.
> The results are promising overall, with the model correctly identifying the true model used to simulate the data—except for the fourth model (both delta_1 and delta_2), which seems to suffer from identifiability issues even in standard MCMC settings.
> However, I’m encountering convergence issues when assessing the chains using Brooks' chi-square tests (https://www.jstor.org/stable/1391067). The p-values don’t increase steadily as simulations progress, and sometimes the chains fail to converge.

Hello nimble community,

I am trying to run a multievent CMR model where we are interested in the effect of age on the seasonal survival of a population of gulls. Because I would eventually like to estimate time-dependent survival and 'age' is an individual time-varying covariate, the state transition matrix is indexed by time and by individual, making it into a very large array when theres a lot of individuals. The event matrix is also time-dependent, making it into another quite large array. This uses lots of memory and I would like to reduce memory usage.

In an attempt to do this, I tweaked the source code of the dDHMMo distribution in order to get rid of some static lines (that are not really time-dependent) in the state transition and event observation matrices. Basically, I followed the steps proposed by Perry on this post <https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/THnkvlENYPc/m/XK56zFjKAAAJ>.

Perry's suggestions for the transition matrix worked great and the model runs fine when only the state transition bit is modified (by the way thanks for that Perry, I didn't end up using it for the model on the original post, but this has been on my mind since then and I'm glad I finally managed to make it work! :)). My attempt at modifying the function further to get rid of some lines in the event array also works fine when I test the code outside of nimble. The function works, and the log probs returned by this tweaked function are identical to those returned by the original verison of dDHMMo. However, when I run the compiled version using the compiledMCMC$run(...) function, R systematically crashes. Because this returns no error, it has been difficult for me to troubleshoot :'(

For information I'm using R version 4.4.0, nimble version 1.1.0, and nimbleEcology 0.4.1

I've attached a reproducible code and an excerpt of the data so that anyone interested could try and reproduce the situation and with some luck someone has an idea of how I would go about solving this. Basically the first lines up to 60 are just setup code, in lines 65-233 are the two versions of dDHMMo I tweaked (in the first one  only transitions are tweaked, in the second both transitions and observations are tweaked), on l.238-342 are the tests with the three dDHMMo distributions outside of model code to ensure all outputs match the original dDHMMo function, 347-568 is two model codes each set up with one of the tweaked distributions and finally 570-670 is code to build/compile/run the MCMC with each model code, with the one that crashes at the end.

Any help is welcome!

Cheers,

Fred L.

Also, relatively unrelated but the first check of dDHMMo is:

    if (length(init) != dim(probObs)[1]) stop("In dDHMMo: Length of init does not match ncol of probObs in dDHMMo.")

Hello Andreas,

A bit difficult to give you an option without knowing what the possible values of z are in your code. A bit more details about your code would help. If the only possible values of z are 1 and 2 you could simply put

Infection[i,f[i]] <- z[i,f[i]] - 1

#Outside of model code, with your data being y:

initial.infection<-rep(NA, times=N)

for(i in 1:N){

}

... all the constants...,

initial.infection)

Inside of model code:

for (i in 1:N){

  # Define latent state at first occasion
  z[i, f[i]] <- y[i, f[i]]

  # Indicator variable with 0 or 1 if infection is absent or present

  Infection[i,f[i]] <- initial.infection[i]

}

Cheers,

Fred

The short answer is no, and that's primarily because nimble allows you to write your own functions and distributions rather than using tricks like this for density calculations. nimble also supports WAIC. I'm not sure what the weighting scheme is here. The quickest way to make your code work in the way it is written would be to provide logdensity.bin as a user-defined function in nimble. It would look like this:

logdensity.bin <- nimbleFunction(
  function(y = double(), p = double(), size = double()) {
    return(dbin(y, prob = p, size = size, log = TRUE))
    returnType(double())
  })
You could hard-code the 1 instead of taking the size argument if you want.

I hope that makes sense. In case you haven't poked around our documentation, the User Manual at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org> has much more about writing your own ("user-defined") functions and distributions to use in models. As noted above I suspect there will be a cleaner way to do what you want. HTH!

Perry

Hi Fred,

Thanks for the question and I'm glad to see this approach. I can reproduce the crash, although I had to run it slightly longer to do so. (You could provide a set.seed to make it more perfectly reproducible.)

I'm going to send a few suggestions but I'm going to stop short of trying to fix and test it myself.

One place I see trouble is here:

      Zpi <- probObs[1:2, xt, t] * pi[1:2] # Vector of P(state) * P(observation class x[t] | state)
      Zpi[3] <- probObs.l3[xt] * pi[3]     # reduced omega to two first lines and keep static lines 3 and 4 to get correct state probabilities
      Zpi[4] <- probObs.l4[xt] * pi[4]

Unlike R, compiled nimbleFunctions will not automatically extend the length of a vector when needed. Here Zpi will become a vector of length 2 from the first line. Then the subsequent lines write beyond its length, which can cause a crash. So you will need to use nimNumeric to create Zpi of the necessary length and then fill its values. Alternatively you could create all four values with c(). This is a mismatch between uncompiled (R) and compiled behavior.

Crashes are almost always caused by writing beyond the size of an object. A strategy for debugging is to run the MCMC uncompiled (i.e. rbgu.MCMC$run(...) ). In your case that won't catch the problem because uncompiled execution (i.e. R) *will* automatically extend the length of a vector when needed. So to catch errors you could add various checks (that you don't expect to need or even work when compiling, e.g. "if(length(Zpi) < 4) browser()"). That can help when it is more obscure where such a problem occurs, but in this case it seems that maybe it just wasn't what you expected.

HTH and let us know if you're still stuck.

Thanks for catching that weird error-trap with the row vs col mixup. I think the actual check is correct and the message needs to say "nrow" instead of "ncol".

Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi nimble community,

I’m currently working on a large life cycle model and encountered an issue I’ve seen mentioned in this group before :

[Warning] There are 131 individual pWAIC values that are greater than 0.4. This may indicate that the WAIC estimate is unstable (Vehtari et al., 2017), at least in cases without grouping of data nodes or multivariate data nodes.

To address this, I’ve already run the model with an extended burn-in phase and a large number of iterations, suspecting convergence might be the root of the problem. However, the warning persists.

My first question is : Is there a way to pinpoint the specific data nodes responsible for pWAIC values exceeding 0.4? The getWAICdetails() function doesn’t seem to provide this information, but it would be very helpful for debugging.

To try debugging this here’s an overview of the types of data nodes in my model:
Abundance :
for (t in 1:C) {
  Eff[t] ~ dlnorm(meanlog = Log_Mu[t], sdlog = Log_Sd[t])
}
- Eff[t] is an abundance estimate derived from a CMR model.
- Log_Sd[t] represents uncertainty in abundance, incorporated as a constant.
Sex ratio :

for (t in 1:C) {
  Nsex[t, 1:2] ~ dmulti(size = Tot[t], prob = Psex[t, 1:2])
}
- Nsex[t] is the number of individuals in each sex.
- Tot[t] is the total number of individuals, treated as a constant.
Size structure :

for (t in 1:C) {
  for (l in 1:L) {
    Scales[l, t] ~ dnorm(mean = Mu[t], sd = Sd[t])
  }
}
- Scales[l, t] represents individual scale lengths over time.
- These values are assumed to follow a normal size distribution defined by Mu[t] and Sd[t].

I suspect the size structure nodes might be causing the issue due to their multivariate nature. From what I’ve read, grouping multivariate nodes for WAIC calculation could be a solution.

My second question is : Would grouping multivariate nodes be a good approach here, or should I abandon WAIC entirely and use another metric like PSIS-LOO, as recommended in the literature ?

Thanks in advance for your insights and advice !

Have a great day,
Eliot B.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am working on a model where I am trying to estimate some unknown ages within a hazard model that has an age effect. The code goes as follows:

# Create a nimble model
sim_code <- nimbleCode({

  #------------------------#
  # Hazard model Priors ####
  #------------------------#

  # Overall log hazard term using param expansion
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  mix ~ dunif(-1, 1)
  log_haz <- beta0 * mix

  # Estimate ages for each unknown animal
  for(i in 1:uniques){
    year_age[i] ~ T(dbinom(10, prob = 0.65), 4, 10)
    birth_day[i] ~ T(dpois(15), 0, 25)
    start_age[i] <- (year_age[i] * 52) - birth_day[i]
  }

  # Now for each unique one set the date to age vector
  for(i in 1:unknowns){
    age2date[i] ~ dnorm(start[i] - start_age[ind[i]], sd = 1)
  }

  #------------------------------#
  # Set up time effect spline ####
  #------------------------------#

  # Start with prior for b_period
  for(i in 1:nknots_period){
    b_period[i] ~ ddexp(0, tau_period)
  }
  tau_period ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)

  # Now inner product with spline to get the effect
  for(i in 1:nT_period){
    time[i] <- inprod(b_period[1:nknots_period],
                      Z_period[i, 1:nknots_period])
  }

  #-------------------------------#
  # Set up the age effect CGAM ####
  #-------------------------------#

  # Start with prior for b_age_cgam
  for(k in 1:nknots_age_cgam){
    ln_b_age_cgam[k] ~ ddexp(0, tau_age_cgam)
    b_age_cgam[k] <- exp(ln_b_age_cgam[k])
  }
  tau_age_cgam ~ dgamma(0.01,0.01)

  # Now inner product with spline and sum to zero constraint
  for(t in 1:nT_age){
    age_effect_temp[t] <- inprod(b_age_cgam[1:nknots_age_cgam],
                                 Z_age_cgam[t, 1:nknots_age_cgam])
    age[t] <- age_effect_temp[t] - mu_age
  }

  # Get the average for sum to zero constraint
  mu_age <- mean(age_effect_temp[1:nT_age])

  #----------------------------#
  # Likelihood for Hazard ####
  #----------------------------#

  # Likelihood
  for (j in 1:records){
    for (k in left[j]:(right[j] - 1)) {
      UCH[j, k] <- exp(log_haz +
                         time[k] +
                         age[k - age2date[j]])
    }
    SLR[j] <- exp(-sum(UCH[j, left[j]:(right[j] - 1)]))
    censor[j] ~ dbern(SLR[j])
  }
})

Within this model, what I am trying to do is estimate the ages for animals that are older than a certain age. Thus the age2date vector seen at the top of the code is mostly data with NAs at the top of the vector for unknown ages. Here animals can only be born at a certain time during a year, but the modeling structure is being done with a time step of weeks. So to get around that, I have the model estimate year_age and then calculate that back to a weekly age by multiplying that term by 52 and then subtracting what week in the year it was born. This then gives me the age2date term. I originally began with that age2date term being assigned rather than distributed because it seemed appropriate that the variance was wrapped within the year_age and birth_day estimates; however, after some deliberation with my advisor, it seemed like the variable needed to be distributed.

The problem that I am having is that each year_age estimate has zero variance and is only sampling a single number during the entire MCMC process. I have tried a few different things and discovered a few problems with my code, but I have not been able to get it to sample correctly. I am wondering if it has something to do with my model specification. Additionally, I'd like to know if there is anything wrong with using a sd = 0 for the dnorm for the age2date vector since that variance should be wrapped up within the two previous nodes?

Any help would be greatly appreciated!

messages.subject_clean: buildMCMC taking days to run
messages.body_plain:
Hi Erika,

Thanks for sending your full example off-list. Too bad turning off conjugacy checking did not help.

I've taken a look and (as you described) your case is a good-sized spatial capture-recapture model. In SCR models, objects can get large quickly due to distances between every individual and every detector location. Your case also has time and (I think) life stage. This is giving roughly (I think) 10.5 million nodes, some in single variables with 3.4 million nodes. Basically, nimble does not scale well for this problem. Some of the deep rewriting we're doing should help in the future, but that won't help you now.

Have you checked out nimbleSCR <https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=nimbleSCR> and Efficient Estimation of Large-Scale Spatial Capture-Recapture Models <https://doi.org/10.1002/ecs2.3385>? These give nimbleFunctions, more compact data structures, and other tricks that can help a great deal. I also noticed that you could consider removing some of the posterior predictive components and obtaining those later. Also (if I am not being too hasty) the NAs in your data matrix will result in samplers to update those values as missing data. I think there were quite a large proportion of those. If you don't really need those imputed as missing data, you could greatly reduce the number of samplers needed by not including those. Finally I noticed a covariate with many NAs. If you have a way to set up "previous" in a smaller way (because it is quite sparse), that could help.

Sorry I don't have a quicker fix for you.

HTH
Perry

I'm not digging into your model in full depth but that could be worth thinking about. For example, are updates to birth_day[i] or year_age[i] very unlikely to be accepted because they determine the mean of age2date[i], which has sd=1 but the changes in birth_day[i] or year_age[i] could change the mean by much more than 1 or 2, and so never be accepted conditional on the value of age2date[i]? Does something like that seem plausible?

Here is one way you could investigate. Say you have cmodel as the compiled model (so you will need to use a step-by-step workflow to have your hands on cmodel, not a single call to nimbleMCMC). The compiled MCMC will use the compiled model. So after you have run the compiled MCMC, you can then manipulate and explore the compiled model. E.g.

cmodel$calculate() # total log probability.

Then explore the conditional log probability profile that a sampler for birth_day[i] is working in.
e.g. for birth_day[i]:

# use i = 5 for example
vals <- 0:25
current_val <- cmodel$birth_day[5]
deps <- cmodel$getDependencies("birth_day[5]")
logProbs <- numeric(length(vals))
for(i in seq_along(vals)) {
  cmodel$birth_day[5] <- vals[i]
  logProbs[i] <- cmodel$calculate(deps)
}
plot(vals, logProbs, type = "b")

# if what you see is a huge spike at the current_val and everything else much lower, then a sampler is not going to be able to move successfully (if it should). You can continue in this line of thinking and look at and change other values in the model to try to understand why it would be stuck in mixing due to the model structure and/or data.

HTH
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Dear Chris,
thank you very much to you and the Nimble Team for the new version. In line with what you wrote, I tried the barker sampler instead of RW_block ion difficult cases - ones that did not converge well. I did it within the runMCMCbtadjust package. The results of my first attempts on three cases:
- convergence issues were on the whole solved. It seems that on one of the cases there remained a substantial autocorrelation in the MCMC but it seemed better than before - with RW_block
- under Windows, all went fine. On Linux (Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit) - Running under: openSUSE Leap 15.2), the run was OK but then just at the end I had the following error that precluded from getting the MCMC result: it was related to a problem with clearCompiled that I have already reported on this list in the past. So I guess all I need is to allow runMCMCbtadjust not to use clearCompiled - adding an argument for that. This problem did not appear with other samplers.
Sincerely,
Frédéric

> We're pleased to announce the release of version 1.3.0.
>
> Version 1.3.0 provides some new and improved functionality, plus some bug fixes and improved error trapping.
>
> The new and improved functionality includes:
> A new multivariate MCMC sampler, the Barker proposal sampler (`sampler_barker`). We encourage users to try this sampler in place of the block Metropolis `RW_block` sampler and let us know how well it works. The Barker sampler uses gradient information and may improve adaptation behavior, including better mixing when parameters are on different scales or the initial proposal scale is too large.
> An improved Laplace/AGHQ implementation that includes use of the `nlminb` optimizer for both inner and outer optimization (for better optimization performance), improved messaging and output naming, returning the log-likelihood and degrees of freedom for model selection calculations, and unified control of optimization method and other controls at either the build stage or through the `updateSettings` method.
> The addition of the BOBYQA optimization method through `nimOptim`, registered via `nimOptimMethod`.
> In addition to the new and improved functionality above, other bug fixes, improved error trapping, and enhancements include:
> Preventing the use of nimbleFunction method names and nimbleFunction names that conflict with names in the nimble language (DSL).
> More carefully checking for and warning of cases of NaN and non-finite log probability values in various samplers that in some cases may indicate invalid MCMC sampling.
> More carefully handling of NaN and non-finite log probability values in the CRP sampler.
> Error trapping cases of dynamic indices producing a non-scalar result in AD-enabled models and provide a suggested work-around.
> Error trapping use of a non-existent `nimbleList`.
> Preventing use of a single seed when running multiple chains via `runMCMC`.
> Improving messaging related to lack of derivative support for functions.
> Adding information about model macros to the manual.
> Fixing bug in caching values in the CRP sampler when maximum number of clusters is exceeded, which would have caused incorrect sampling (albeit with the user having been warned that they should increase the maximum number of clusters).
> Fixing an issue preventing use of `nimbleList` elements in `nimCat`.
> Preventing an adaptation interval of one for various block samplers for which an interval of one leads to an error.
> Allowing `runLaplace` to use an uncompiled Laplace object.

This is giving roughly (I think) 10.5 million nodes, some in single variables with 3.4 million nodes. Basically, nimble does not scale well for this problem. Some of the deep rewriting we're doing should help in the future, but that won't help you now.

These give nimbleFunctions, more compact data structures, and other tricks that can help a great deal. I also noticed that you could consider removing some of the posterior predictive components and obtaining those later. Also (if I am not being too hasty) the NAs in your data matrix will result in samplers to update those values as missing data. I think there were quite a large proportion of those. If you don't really need those imputed as missing data, you could greatly reduce the number of samplers needed by not including those. Finally I noticed a covariate with many NAs. If you have a way to set up "previous" in a smaller way (because it is quite sparse), that could help.
